newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore shipowners slow to meet new safety rules.
newsitem.headline: Singapore shipowners slow to meet new safety rules.

text.p: More than 40 percent of Singapore-registered ships have yet to apply for new safety certification due to be implemented on July 1, 1998, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said on Monday.

"We are hoping that the remaining 40 or so percent would have got their certification by then... we are very hopeful that that this will happen," Lee Seng Kong, the director of the Shipping Division of the MPA, told Reuters.

MPA, which represents Singapore in the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), is responsible for the implementation of the International Management Code for Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention (International Management Code or ISM).

The ISM Code aims to ensure safety at sea and avoid damage to the environment by requiring ships officers and managers vessels to develop, implement and assess pollution prevention management, according to a set of specific guidelines.

Passenger vessels, tankers, gas and bulk carries and cargo high speed craft of 500 gross tonnage and above, registered in 130 countries which have ratified the 1974 International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) are required to obtain certification of compliance by next year.
The Code will be extended to other types of vessels and mobile offshore drilling units of 500 gross tonnage and above by July 1, 2002.
"More than 20 percent have complied and over 30 percent are in the process," Lee said of the 990 Singapore-registered vessels. "We have one year so there is a little bit of speeding up required."
But setting up the safety management system required by the Code could take as long as two years, said Otto Dijxhoorn of the IMO.
"The consequences for owners who fail to gain ISM accreditation could, to put it mildy, be distinctively unpleasent and lead to interruptions in service," Dijxhoorn said.
He said the ship owner would be in breach of international and national law and the ship may detained.
On the failure to meet the deadline, Lee said "Singapore is a reputable port...we would have to look at it on a case by case basis."
"We want to encourage them (shipowners) to understand and implement the ISM, but they have to take the initiave themselves."
